title: V'Zot HaBerachah: face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10–12)
hook: no prophet arose like Moses, "whom the LORD knew face to face"

segments.voice: Yesterday in V'Zot HaBerachah, the grave no one knows. Your line was no grave, only teaching. What did you pass on, and in whose name? Today, the Torah's last word about Moses himself. Day five hundred thirty-six.

A teacher stays after class to explain it one more time. A coach sees something in a kid before the kid does. A grandparent explains the world over breakfast. People like this rarely ask for credit, and often never hear what they did. Their names fade, while what they taught keeps going. The Torah's final verses are, in a way, a tribute to a teacher. They say who Moses was, now that he's gone.
screen: `A TEACHER AFTER CLASS.` → `A GRANDPARENT AT BREAKFAST.` → `A TRIBUTE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: "And there hath not arisen a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face." Then the verses recall the signs in Egypt and the mighty hand, done in the sight of all Israel. Face to face: in Hebrew, panim el panim. Earlier, in Numbers, God explains the difference to Moses' own brother and sister: with other prophets I speak in visions and dreams, but with Moses, mouth to mouth. The text presents that closeness as direct, unlike any other. Maimonides made that uniqueness one of his thirteen principles of faith: that Moses' prophecy stands above that of every other prophet. And yet, notice the title Jewish tradition actually gives him. Not Moses our prophet. Not Moses our king. Moshe Rabbenu: Moses our teacher. He led slaves out of Egypt, stood at the sea, met God on a mountain, and the name that stuck is teacher. There's a quiet second meaning in face to face. It describes something no one else had: God and Moses. But a teacher is known face to face too, by the students sitting across the table. In the tradition, Moses' closeness to God reaches later generations through what he taught. The book closes, and the tribute it chooses is this: he was known, close up. And through him, so were the words.
screen: `NO PROPHET SINCE LIKE MOSES.` · `PANIM EL PANIM.` · `MAIMONIDES' SEVENTH PRINCIPLE.` · `MOSHE RABBENU: MOSES OUR TEACHER.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a teacher who shaped you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a teacher of any kind. A schoolteacher, a rabbi, a boss, a parent, an older friend. See their face, close up. What did they give you that you still use? Thank them in your mind. Then ask yourself whether you could tell them for real. A message, a letter, a call. If they've died, tell someone else about them, by name. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. Ending with Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher.
Your line: face to face. Today, thank a teacher who shaped you, directly if you can, or tell someone about them. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: In Jewish speech Moses is commonly called Moshe Rabbenu, 'Moses our teacher', and the closing verses of Deuteronomy are read on Simchat Torah as the yearly Torah cycle ends.

fork.setup: Moses freed slaves, led a nation and spoke with God. which title does Jewish tradition give him?
fork.reveal: Moshe Rabbenu: of everything he did, the name that stuck is teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: they met in person.
what it means: a direct closeness to God no other prophet had, and a man remembered above all as a teacher.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 12:6–8 contrasts visions and dreams with 'mouth to mouth'; Maimonides' seventh principle is the uniqueness of Moses' prophecy.
